instructional_purpose: Establishes sentence-level grammar as a named discipline with its own object of study, motivates it by showing that final-vowel marking rather than word order carries who-does-what, and situates it beside the word-form discipline. The lesson is orientation and terminology rather than a procedure the learner can execute.
concepts_taught: the sentence-level discipline as a named science with a defined object
final-vowel marking as the carrier of grammatical role
role reversal when two endings are exchanged in a verb-initial clause
the three case labels and the short vowel conventionally paired with each
division of labour between the sentence discipline and the word-form discipline
historical motivation: safeguarding correct reading for learners coming to the language from outside it

linguistic_propositions.proposition: In a verb-initial clause the grammatical roles are signalled by the final vowel of each nominal rather than by their linear order, so exchanging the two vowels exchanges the roles.
The nominative vowel identifies the doer, the accusative vowel the undergoer, and the genitive vowel possession or the complement of a preposition.
The sentence discipline governs relations between words while the word-form discipline governs the internal build of a single word.
Verb form varies to express tense, degree of certainty and command.
The discipline was founded by a named early figure who also devised the vowel-pointing system, and its earliest comprehensive treatise is by a named second-century author.

recognition_criteria: a clause in which two nominals carry different final short vowels while the verb precedes both
the same word appearing with different final vowels across occurrences
a nominal standing immediately after a preposition
procedures: read the final vowel of each nominal before assigning any role
assign doer and undergoer from the vowel rather than from position
sort a question into word-internal or sentence-level before deciding which discipline answers it
conditions: fully vowelled text
nominals whose ending is visible and regularly marked by a short vowel
exceptions: words whose ending never varies, and words whose state is shown by a letter rather than a short vowel, are not addressed at this stage
contrasts: role assignment by ending versus role assignment by word order as in English
sentence-level discipline versus word-form discipline
the three case labels against one another
misleading_shortcuts: equating the nominative vowel with the doer, when the same vowel also marks topics, predicates and other non-agent positions
equating the genitive vowel with possession, when it is licensed by prepositions and by annexation generally
assuming any swap of two endings yields a well-formed clause with the reverse meaning
worked_analysis_stages: present a minimal pair differing only in the two final vowels
read the reversed roles off the endings
name the resulting semantic reversal
paradigms: a three-row case-label table pairing each label with its default short vowel and a typical function
exercise_types: multiple choice on terminology and on the discipline split
multiple choice on historical attribution
single-word translation recall
case-function identification from a vowelled minimal pair
fill-in-the-blank completion of the discipline's definition
prerequisite_knowledge: the Arabic script and the three short vowel marks
ability to read a fully vowelled clause aloud
reuses_from_earlier: letters and vowel marks from the preceding module
new_knowledge: the name and scope of the sentence-level discipline
case endings presented as a meaning-bearing system rather than decoration
the discipline split that the rest of the module leans on

instructional_purpose: Draws the technical line between a single lexical unit and a string that counts as speech in the grammarians' sense, and states three conditions that must hold jointly for the stronger label to apply. The purpose is to fix a metalinguistic threshold before any sentence analysis begins.
concepts_taught: single word versus technically complete utterance
compositeness requirement stated as a minimum of two words
informativeness requirement stated as conveying a complete thought
conventionality requirement stated as arrangement by the language's own conventions
fragment recognition: multi-word strings that still fail the threshold
a finite verb carrying an incorporated subject pronoun still counts as one word

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A string counts as speech in the technical sense only if compositeness, informativeness and conventionality all hold.
Compositeness requires at least two words.
A verb inflected for a first-person subject is nonetheless a single word, not a composite.
A string opened by a conditional particle and left without its consequent fails the informativeness condition.
Isolated one-word calls used communicatively in a market are words but not speech.
A definite noun followed by an indefinite predicate constitutes a complete assertion.

recognition_criteria: count the independent words in the string
test whether a hearer is left waiting for a completion
test whether the arrangement follows the language's conventions rather than being arbitrary sound
check whether the string can stand as an answer that ends the exchange
procedures: apply the three conditions in fixed order and reject on the first failure
when rejecting, name which condition failed rather than judging by feel
conditions: all three requirements must hold simultaneously
the string is taken in isolation, without contextual completion
exceptions: imperatives and other forms whose subject is implicit, treated by classical analysis as complete through an estimated pronoun, are not reconciled with the stated two-word minimum
elliptical answers recoverable from the preceding turn are excluded by the stated criteria although speakers treat them as complete
clitics and pronouns written joined to their host make the word count depend on segmentation, which the lesson does not address
contrasts: word versus utterance
multi-word fragment versus complete assertion
everyday sense of speech versus the technical definition of the same term

common_mistakes.pattern: treating any meaningful word as an instance of technical speech
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the technical term requires composition into a complete proposition, not mere meaningfulness
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply all three conditions before applying the label

common_mistakes.pattern: accepting a multi-word string as speech because it contains more than one word
common_mistakes.why_wrong: word count alone does not satisfy informativeness; a string opened by a conditional particle leaves the proposition unfinished
common_mistakes.correction_principle: test for a completed proposition rather than for word count

common_mistakes.pattern: importing the ordinary sense of the word speech into the technical term
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the technical term is narrower and is defined by three joint conditions
common_mistakes.correction_principle: keep the technical definition separate from the ordinary sense of the same lexeme

misleading_shortcuts: treating two words as a sufficient test for the label
assuming any string containing a verb is complete
assuming the word boundary coincides with orthographic spacing, when attached particles and pronouns are written joined
worked_analysis_stages: take a candidate string
test compositeness, then informativeness, then conventionality
label pass or fail and name the failing condition
paradigms: a three-row condition table naming each requirement and its plain-language content
a two-column pass/fail classification table over candidate strings
exercise_types: multiple choice classification of strings as qualifying or not
multiple choice on the number and identity of the conditions
terminology recall in free-response form
vocabulary translation recall
fill-in-the-blank completion of the condition list
prerequisite_knowledge: reading vowelled Arabic
the notion that individual words carry meaning

new_knowledge: a technical threshold for what counts as an analysable utterance, with three joint conditions and named fragment types
sarf_relevance: none - the lesson contains no word-form material
nahw_relevance: medium - it fixes the utterance boundary that all sentence analysis presupposes, but supplies no structural criterion beyond word count and intuition of completeness
tutor_drill_relevance: good source for a classify-the-string drill in which the learner must name the failing condition rather than answer yes or no
rich_hover_relevance: low - hover operates on a token occurrence, while this material operates on whole strings
corpus_pvn_relevance: indirect for p/v/n entries; bears on segmenting a passage into analysable utterances rather than on entry content, and would matter only if a consumer had to decide whether a span forms a complete assertion

instructional_purpose: Introduces the word-form discipline by contrast with the sentence discipline, then demonstrates the consonantal-core-plus-template mechanism through one root's word family, including the template that commonly yields a noun of place.
concepts_taught: scope of the word-form discipline against the sentence discipline
the consonantal core as the carrier of a shared meaning field
the template as a slot pattern of vowels and added letters
template-to-function mapping, with مَفْعَل presented as a place noun
the initial م of that template as template material rather than a radical
recovering the core from a derived surface form

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The word-form discipline studies how a single word is built, while the sentence discipline studies how words relate inside a sentence.
Arabic words are built by placing a consonantal core into a template.
Words sharing a core are related in meaning.
The initial م of a place noun on this template belongs to the template, not to the core.
The مَفْعَل template commonly denotes the place at which the action occurs.
The gloss given in a vocabulary table is the word's translation.

recognition_criteria: a set of words whose consonants recur in the same order under different vowel patterns
an initial م standing before three surviving consonants that fill the template's slots
a residual letter that has no slot in the core once the template is matched
procedures: remove template material and read off the consonantal core
fit the core into a named template and predict the function class from the template
when a question is about build, answer with the word-form discipline; when it is about the ending in a sentence, answer with the sentence discipline
conditions: a triliteral core recoverable from the surface
a known template inventory to match against
exceptions: place versus time reading inside the same م-template is not decided by the template alone and the lesson does not raise the distinction
cores whose consonants are hidden by weakness or gemination are not addressed
words with no productive derivational core, such as particles and primitive nouns, are not excluded from the stated generalisation
contrasts: a build question versus a sentence-function question
core letters versus template letters, specifically the initial م
two words on different templates from one core

common_mistakes.pattern: answering a word-build question with a sentence-function analysis, or the reverse
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two disciplines have different objects, so the wrong one supplies no criterion for the question asked
common_mistakes.correction_principle: classify the question by whether it concerns the inside of a word or its role in a sentence, then choose the discipline

common_mistakes.pattern: counting a template's initial م among the core consonants
common_mistakes.why_wrong: that م fills a template slot and is not owned by the core, so the derived core would be four letters and false
common_mistakes.correction_principle: assign every surface letter either to a core slot or to the template, and never by shape alone

common_mistakes.pattern: treating any three adjacent consonants in a word as its core
common_mistakes.why_wrong: some of those letters are inflectional or template material, so adjacency does not establish ownership
common_mistakes.correction_principle: certify the core against the template inventory rather than reading it off the surface

misleading_shortcuts: an initial م always signals template material
a shared core licenses a shared translation
the typical sense of a template holds for every word built on it
worked_analysis_stages: take one consonantal core
list the words derived from it with their templates
label each derived word by function class
paradigms: a single-core derivation table pairing template names with function labels: past verb, imperfect verb, place noun, container noun, patient participle, agent participle
exercise_types: multiple choice on the discipline split and on template function
multiple choice on core identification inside a derived word

free-response translation recall
fill-in-the-blank contrasting the two disciplines

ability to read vowelled derived forms

unit_mapping.equivalence_basis: u-s01 was authored from this lesson and names L1.M2.03 as its only lesson_ref, and the lesson's extractable claims are already in the ledger as cl-001 (discipline split), cl-002 (every word from a core and template), cl-003 (core-sharing implies related meaning), cl-012 (vocabulary gloss as translation) and cl-015 (the initial م as template material). instructional_purpose: Establishes that every word falls into exactly one of three classes, defines each class by its own criterion (naming without time, action anchored in time, meaning only in combination), and maps the eight-way English scheme onto that three-way division.
concepts_taught: the three-way exhaustive division of words
the naming class defined by reference without inherent time
the action class defined by an event anchored to a time
the residual class defined by having no meaning in isolation
positive markers offered per class: the definite article and nunation for the first, conjugation and time reference for the second
the mapping of English adjectives, pronouns and adverbs onto the naming class and of prepositions and conjunctions onto the residual class
the three time frames of the action class and their names
a clause containing no explicit action word treated as noun-initial

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Every word belongs to exactly one of three classes, with no remainder.
A word of the naming class denotes an entity without carrying a time reference.
A word of the action class denotes an event bound to past, present or command.
A word of the residual class carries meaning only when combined with something else and cannot stand as an answer to a question.
What English classes as adjective, pronoun and interjection is a subtype of the naming class and inflects like it.
An adverb corresponds sometimes to the naming class and sometimes to the residual class.
A word naming a time point belongs to the naming class despite denoting time, because it does not denote an event.
A sentence beginning with a noun and containing no explicit action word is a noun-initial sentence.

recognition_criteria: the word accepts the definite article or nunation, which points to the naming class
the word conjugates for person, number and gender and takes the imperfect prefixes, which points to the action class
the word cannot stand alone as an answer and shows neither of the above, which points to the residual class
the word carries an inherent time frame, which excludes the naming class
procedures: for each word in a clause, test for the naming markers, then for conjugation and time, then assign the remainder to the residual class
state the reason for the assignment alongside the label
conditions: the word is taken as a full word rather than a fragment
the test is applied to a vowelled written form
exceptions: borderline items disputed among grammarians, such as verb-like nouns and certain negators, are not raised
the claim of exhaustiveness is asserted without discussing which items force the debate
contrasts: naming class versus action class, discriminated by inherent time reference
residual class versus the other two, discriminated by inability to stand alone
the three-way Arabic division versus the eight-way English scheme
an event word versus the noun naming the same event, which lacks time
misleading_shortcuts: assuming a word that translates as an English adjective or adverb must belong to a separate class
treating the definite-article test as the whole diagnostic, when many nouns are excluded from it in a given occurrence
reading the absence of an explicit action word as proof of a noun-initial sentence type without checking the predicate
assuming a word naming a time must belong to the action class
worked_analysis_stages: take a short clause
assign each word to one of the three classes
give a one-clause reason per word
observe from the assignment that the clause contains no action word and classify the sentence type
paradigms: a three-row class table pairing each class with its definition and marker set
a three-row time-frame table for the action class
an eight-row English-to-Arabic class mapping table
exercise_types: multiple choice class assignment for a given word

sarf_relevance: medium - class membership is a precondition for template classification, and the action-class time frames anticipate the tense/aspect stems, but no formation rule is taught
nahw_relevance: high - the class assignment is the first gate of every syntactic decision and every later sign inventory in the module
tutor_drill_relevance: strong basis for a label-plus-reason drill over each word of a short clause, with credit withheld when the reason is wrong even if the label is right
rich_hover_relevance: high - a hover gloss must commit to one of these three classes before any further analysis, and the English-mapping table prevents surfacing a foreign category label

uncertainty_flags: the no-exceptions claim about exhaustiveness is stated without the disputed borderline items grammarians debate

proposed_new_units.summary: assignment of a token to the naming, action or residual class, with the per-class positive definitions and the mapping that blocks importing English categories; this lesson contributes the class definitions and the mapping, while L1.M2.05 to L1.M2.07 contribute the sign inventories

instructional_purpose: Supplies the positive sign inventory for the naming class: five markers any one of which is sufficient for the label, each justified by the systematic failure of the other two classes to accept it, and applied to two borderline items.
concepts_taught: five sufficient markers for the naming class
the definite article as a marker restricted to that class
nunation as a marker restricted to indefinite members of that class
position after a preposition as a marker, with the resulting genitive state
the vocative particle يا as a marker
occupying the subject position of a predication as a marker
sufficiency: one marker settles the label, no marker is mandatory
the exclusion argument: the action and residual classes fail every marker

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Accepting any one of the five markers is sufficient to classify a word in the naming class.
The definite article attaches only to words of the naming class.
Nunation appears only on indefinite words of the naming class, in three vowel shapes matching the three states.
Only a word of the naming class may follow a preposition, and it then stands in the genitive.
Only a word of the naming class may be addressed with the vocative particle, and a called proper name then takes a bare nominative without nunation.
Only a word of the naming class can be the element about which something is predicated.
A word naming the present moment accepts nunation and takes a genitive vowel after a preposition, and is therefore of the naming class.
A demonstrative rejects the article and nunation yet is of the naming class on the strength of the predication test alone.

recognition_criteria: the word carries the definite article
the word carries a doubled final vowel
the word stands immediately after a preposition
the word stands immediately after the vocative particle as the one being called
the word occupies the position about which a comment is made
procedures: run the five markers in order and stop at the first that the word accepts
when no marker is directly visible, construct a frame in which the word would appear and test acceptability
for a word rejecting the article and nunation, fall back to the predication test before concluding
conditions: the word is examined in or against a licensing frame rather than in isolation
a single accepted marker suffices; the absence of the other four is not evidence against the label
exceptions: members of the naming class that reject the article and nunation still belong to it, so absence of markers is not disconfirming
a preposition may govern a subordinated clause whose head is not of the naming class, which the exclusive formulation of the preposition test does not accommodate
words of the naming class with fixed endings do not display the state that the preposition test predicts
contrasts: a naming-class word against an action-class word across all five markers
a naming-class word against a residual-class word across all five markers
the definite and indefinite realisation of the same word
a word bearing multiple markers against one bearing only the predication marker

common_mistakes.pattern: concluding that a word is not of the naming class because it rejects the article and nunation
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the markers are sufficient rather than necessary, so failing four of them proves nothing
common_mistakes.correction_principle: continue to the remaining markers, and treat one acceptance as decisive

common_mistakes.pattern: classifying a demonstrative outside the naming class because it takes neither the article nor nunation
common_mistakes.why_wrong: demonstratives are a subtype of the naming class and are diagnosed by the predication test
common_mistakes.correction_principle: use the predication test as the fallback marker for words with fixed shapes

common_mistakes.pattern: treating a word that denotes a time as belonging to the action class
common_mistakes.why_wrong: denoting a time is not the same as denoting an event anchored in time
common_mistakes.correction_principle: diagnose by marker acceptance rather than by what the word denotes

misleading_shortcuts: treating the article test as necessary rather than sufficient
assuming a word with no visible marker in a given occurrence has no class
assuming a genitive vowel is always present after a preposition, when fixed-ending words show none
generalising from the sufficiency rule that any marker may be attached to any member of the class

paradigms: a five-row marker table pairing each marker with its Arabic name and an instance

instructional_purpose: Supplies the positive sign inventory for the action class, pairing each marker with the stem it attaches to and, for one marker, with a meaning that shifts by stem; closes with the same exclusion argument used for the naming class.
concepts_taught: a marker set sufficient for the action class
the particle قد and its stem-sensitive reading
the prefixed and free future markers, both restricted to the imperfect stem
the silent feminine ending on the perfect stem
the vowelled subject ending on the perfect stem and its person paradigm
the addressee-feminine ending on the imperfect stem
the emphatic ending in heavy and light shapes
the distinction between the two perfect-stem endings by whether the consonant carries a vowel

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Accepting any one of the listed markers is sufficient to classify a word in the action class.
The particle قد conveys completion or emphasis on the perfect stem and possibility on the imperfect stem.
Both future markers attach only to the imperfect stem.
The prefixed future marker signals nearer futurity and the free one signals more distant or more emphatic futurity.
The vowelless final consonant ending marks a feminine subject on the perfect stem, and the naming class marks feminine differently.
The vowelled final consonant ending marks a first or second person subject on the perfect stem and varies by person, number and gender.
The addressee-feminine marker replaces the final consonant of the standard imperfect form.
The emphatic ending exists in a heavy and a light shape, the light one being confined to elevated and classical registers.
Words of the naming and residual classes accept none of these markers.

recognition_criteria: the word is immediately preceded by the completion particle
the word carries a future prefix or is preceded by the free future word
the word ends in a vowelless consonant marking a feminine subject
the word ends in a vowelled consonant matching one of the person endings
the word ends in the addressee-feminine sequence
the word carries the emphatic ending, usually with an introductory prefix or under an oath
procedures: identify the stem as perfect or imperfect before applying a marker, since several markers are stem-restricted
for a final consonant ending, check whether it bears a vowel to decide between the feminine and the subject reading
tabulate which markers are attested and which are merely possible for the word under test
conditions: the stem type must be known for the stem-restricted markers
vowelling must be visible for the two consonant endings to be told apart
exceptions: the reading given for the completion particle on the imperfect stem does not cover its frequency reading, and its reading on the perfect stem does not cover proximity
the emphatic ending's interaction with the stem's final vowel and with intervening particles is not stated
the addressee-feminine account is stated in a way its own paradigm contradicts, so the exception space is undefined
contrasts: completion particle on the perfect stem versus on the imperfect stem
the vowelless feminine ending versus the vowelled subject ending, discriminated by the presence of a vowel

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A word that rejects the article, nunation and all verbal markers belongs to the residual class.
A word of the residual class signifies only in combination with another word.
A preposition places the following noun in the genitive state.
The word after a coordinator takes the same state as the word before it.
لم negates past time while selecting the imperfect stem.
لن negates future time.
The negator ما negates the perfect stem only dialectally.
Only the two yes-no particles are interrogatives of this class; content interrogatives belong to the naming class because they can occupy argument positions.
The coordinator meaning and can also introduce a circumstantial clause or an oath, so its function is context-determined.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A consonantal core carries a core meaning shared by every word derived from it.
The template determines the word's function class: verb, agent, patient, place or abstract.
The placeholder letters ف, ع and ل stand for the first, second and third core consonants in order.
فاعِل yields the one performing the action and مَفْعول the one undergoing it.
مَفْعَل yields the place at which the action occurs.
Knowing a core and a template lets a learner form words never encountered before.
Most cores have three consonants but some have four.
Some template-and-core combinations do not exist, so the system organises attested words rather than licensing all combinations.
Some templates add letters that resemble core consonants.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A word is either one whose ending varies with its grammatical function or one whose ending is fixed regardless of position.
Most nouns, descriptive words and imperfect-stem verbs have variable endings.
Personal pronouns, demonstratives, relatives, content interrogatives, perfect-stem verbs and all particles have fixed endings.
Perfect-stem verbs are built on the a-vowel.
The imperfect stem varies because it has several moods while the perfect stem expresses only completion and therefore needs no distinctions.
The complement of a transitive verb of asking stands in the genitive.
High-frequency words were fixed early because context made their function clear without markers.
Knowing which words vary and which do not lets a reader supply endings mentally in unvowelled text.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Inflected words occupy one of four states, each with a primary marker.
Nouns take three of the four states and never the jussive; imperfect-stem verbs take three and never the genitive.
The nominative is the state of the subject of a verb and of both members of a noun-initial predication.
The accusative is the state of the direct object, of the complement of the copular family, of the noun governed by the emphatic family and of a circumstantial element.
The genitive is licensed by a preposition or by annexation and by nothing else.
The imperfect stem is nominative by default and takes accusative or jussive only under a governor.
For weak and five-verb classes the jussive is realised by deletion of the final letter rather than by a vowel marker.
A fatha-ending broken plural following a cardinal numeral inside an annexation is accusative as a specifying complement.
The special noun set and the sound masculine plural show their states by letters rather than by short vowels.

unit_mapping.equivalence_basis: u-n01 already holds the case and mood system with a stricter evidence rule, and u-s06 holds the weak and five-verb classes. What this lesson adds to u-n01 is a class-by-state availability matrix stated as a hard restriction, namely that the genitive is unavailable to verbs and the jussive to nouns, which u-n01 does not record and which functions as a cheap contradiction check on any proposed analysis. It adds to u-s06 the observation that the jussive of those classes is realised by letter deletion rather than by a vowel. Its numeral example is defective and must not be promoted.
